analysis.body: {"transcript": {"text": "Your arguments next in Sutter against Ohio. Court will be sitting for the first time in 1984. In 120 hours. From 10 o'clock. Court will adjourn. Beginning of the 1984 term. 85 term. At 10 hundred hours. Monday, October 1st. That means Monday, October 1st. I'm in the spot back there. Mr. Morrison, I think you may proceed whenever you're ready. Mr. Chief Justice, may it please the court. In 1977, in Bates against the State Bar of Arizona, this court held that the First Amendment limits the ability of states to prohibit truthful advertising by lawyers. I don't know about that, but. It then applied the doctrines for commercial speech, which had been established the prior year in the Virginia pharmacy case. And set aside the discipline imposed on the lawyers who had advertised in that case. Security. Security. In 1982, in RMJ, this court again was faced with a case of lawyer advertising in the mass media. The court again was faced with a case of law enforcement. After reaffirming the four-part test for commercial speech, the court had enunciated two years earlier in the Central Hudson case. The court again set aside the discipline imposed on a lawyer, which had been based on broad prohibitions against lawyer advertising. Two years later, the Ohio Supreme Court, after paying lip service to both Bates and RMJ by stating that they did not prohibit the states from restricting lawyers' advertisements completely, imposed a public reprimand on the appellant, Philip Zouter, because he had run a truthful ad in 36 Ohio newspapers offering to represent women who had been injured as a result of wearing a Dalkon Shield IUD. And he had agreed to represent them on a contingency basis in suits against the manufacturer of the device. The principal basis for reversal in this court is that the Ohio Supreme Court failed to prove that any of the charges against him met the stringent requirements for banning truthful ads that this court has established in commercial speech cases as applied to members of the bar. In order to demonstrate why none of the three charges against Mr. Zouter can be sustained, it's first necessary to describe the ad briefly, and then in some detail to review the specific charges that were made against him. The Dalkon Shield ad appears in several places in the record, most prominently at page 5 of the jurisdictional statement. The ad begins by asking in large capital letters, did you use this IUD? And then below and to the left of the ad is a picture of the Dalkon Shield IUD, which incidentally is quite a different device from other IUDs that were sold by other manufacturers. And hence the picture was a particularly important element in the ad. And the picture is admitted by all to be an accurate representation of a Dalkon Shield. The ad then goes on to discuss specific medical problems that women who used the IUD made by the manufacturer encountered, including problems resulting from unplanned pregnancy as well as other medical disabilities. The ad then went on to point out that it, quote, may not be too late to sue, even though the injuries may have taken place some time ago, which is a correct statement of the law of Ohio, because it has a very liberal statute of limitations with respect to its tolling provisions in injuries of this kind. Following that, there was a discussion of the fact that the appellate, Mr. Zauder, was representing women in cases like this and that he was prepared to represent others on a contingent fee basis, followed by his name, his address, and a telephone number. Now, in light of the accuracy of this ad, it's not surprising that the appellate, the disciplinary counsel of the Supreme Court of Ohio, stipulated that the ad, and I am now quoting, does not contain a false, fraudulent, misleading, deceptive, self-laudatory, or unfair statement or claim. Now, despite this stipulation, the appellate has charged appellate with multiple violations of the Ohio Code of Professional Responsibility, and the Ohio Supreme Court has sustained those charges in three separate respects. The first group of these charges were violations of the Code's anti-solicitation provisions. Now, there are two related provisions in the Ohio Code. One prohibits lawyers from recommending themselves for employment to a layperson who has not requested their advice. And now, according to the Ohio Supreme Court, that applies even though the solicitation in question here took place solely through newspapers of general circulation in Ohio. The second and related solicitation charge is that the appellant here gave unsolicited legal advice, presumably the advice that it may not be too late to sue, and that the appellant then accepted employment based upon his advertisement which contained that advice. And once again, the Ohio Supreme Court applied that restriction to newspaper ads of general circulation. The second set of charges involving the Dalkon Shield ad against the appellant related to the fact that he put in his ad an accurate illustration of the Dalkon Shield. Under the Ohio Code, it is a violation to include any illustration other than a picture of the lawyer himself or herself or a portrait of the scales of justice. Since appellant plainly violated that restriction, the only question with that has been from the start whether that broad prohibition violates the First Amendment. The third set of charges involving this ad relate to the contingent fee portion of the ad. The Ohio Supreme Court did not criticize appellant for what he said in the ad, but for what he failed to include. According to the Ohio Supreme Court's Code of Professional Responsibility, for those lawyers who advertise in contingent fee cases, there are two affirmative disclosure requirements that must be contained in each ad involving a contingent fee. First, if the lawyer uses the word contingent fees at all, the lawyer must include the actual rates or the percentages charged. And that is true regardless of how many rates the lawyer has or whether the lawyer charges different fees under different circumstances. All those rates must be disclosed in the ad itself. Second, in addition, in all advertisements for contingent fees, the lawyer must state whether the percentage taken by the lawyer is before or after expenses. And that is true even where the lawyer, as in this case, did not mention any percentages at all. So in both cases, the mere mention of the term contingent fees triggers two affirmative disclosure requirements under the Ohio Code. Before proceeding to the specific charges, I want to say a word about the benefits that this advertisement conferred because, as this court has recognized in the Virginia Pharmacy case, Bates, and many other cases involving commercial speech, that benefits are an important element and that the benefits accrue not only to the speaker but also to the listener or the reader. And here, in that case, it is principally women who had used Dalkon Shield IUDs at some prior time. Here, we need not speculate about potential benefits because the record at the trial in this proceeding amply demonstrates that there were real benefits to real people that directly resulted from this ad. Now, among those who benefited are the nearly 100 women who contacted appellant after they had read the ad and after conferring with him, agreed to have him represent them in their lawsuit to recover for these very damaging injuries from the manufacturer of the IUD. For some, like Beverly Carr, the advertisement was the first time that she learned of the connection between the Dalkon Shield and the injuries that she had suffered. And for her, the key element in the ad was the picture of the Dalkon Shield because she testified that she ordinarily does not read the words in written advertisements and it was the illustration that got her attention. That's perfectly consistent with Mr. Zauderer's own testimony where he told the tribunal that he had previously run an ad for Dalkon Shield plaintiffs. Mr. Morrison, would you make the same argument if the illustration in an ad by a lawyer trying to represent personal injury victims showed the face of a happy person carrying home bags of money? Well, I certainly would say that the analysis would have to be the same, that the commercial speech test would have to be the same. We would have to identify the interest being asserted. We would then have to determine whether that interest is directly advanced by a prohibition. And third, whether there are less restrictive alternatives. I know that it won't satisfy Your Honor's question, but I don't think that the public is going to accept those kind of ads, that the public expects something different from a lawyer. My own view, without having heard what the state's interest would be other than the fact that the ad was not dignified, and I certainly would agree that it wasn't a dignified ad, but don't believe that the First Amendment would allow the state to make that kind of determination. In the absence of hearing some rather strong determination and strong interest, I would say the state could not prohibit that ad, principally because I don't think there's much harm likely to occur. Yes, it's not very good for the legal profession, and I, as a lawyer, might resent some member of the bar running an ad like that, but I don't think that's a reason that our Constitution allows the suppression of speech, even in a commercial context. Now, in addition to people like Beverly Carr who learned about the connection for the first time, there were others who benefited in similar but somewhat different ways, and that is Kay Carver, who also testified as a client of Mr. Zadler's. For her, this ad meant the difference between good legal advice and bad legal advice. She had previously been to a lawyer who had told her that it was too late to sue the manufacturer, that the statute had already run, and that her only remedy was a medical malpractice action against her doctor, which she didn't want to bring because the problem was not from the doctor. She went to see Mr. Zadler after reading his ad and learning that it may not be too late, and she has thus been able to go to court and vindicate her rights as a direct result of this ad. Now, beyond the individuals whom Mr. Zadler represented, there was another larger group of persons who were benefited from this ad, and those were women who, like Beverly Carr, learned for the first time that the Dalkon shield may be a dangerous product and may... Mr. Morrison, may I ask you, have there been recoveries in any of these cases? Yes, there have been recoveries and there have been settlements also. If Your Honor is referring to Mr. Zadler, I believe that he has had no case to go to judgment yet, but he has had some of his cases have been settled. But there have been judgments in other cases involving the Dalkon shield. Now, the second group of beneficiaries are the women who, as a result of seeing this ad, have gone to their physicians, have been examined to determine whether they are wearing a Dalkon shield IUD. And this is necessitated by the fact that the manufacturer stopped producing the product and selling it in 1974. But many women, according to plaintiff's expert obstetrician, continue to have Dalkon shields in them and are continuously at risk from the dangers that the shield can produce. And it's very important that women who have them go to their doctors and see whether, if they are there, and if so, they should be taken out. And many women today that Dr. Halle sees do not know about the danger. And many women who saw this ad learned about the danger and, as a result, are in a better position to protect their personal health and probably avoid lawsuits over the device. How long prohibits a physician from putting essentially the same ad in the paper saying, come and see me? I do not know the answer to that question. Dr. Halle testified that physicians couldn't do what Mr. Zauderer did here. From that, I took the inference that he may believe that that law prohibits it, but it would seem to me that that law, if there is such a law in Ohio, I would be as unconstitutional as the prohibitions are here, that there are real public benefits from people knowing about it. In addition, I would point out now, Mr. Chief Justice, that the A.H. Robbins Company has recently run an advertisement, not simply for doctors, but in the general publications, which is attached as an addendum to our reply brief, urging all women who believe that they may have a Dalkon shield in them to see their physicians, and Robbins is prepared to pay for the cost of doing the work. In addition, you will note that the ad contains an illustration of the Dalkon shield virtually identical to the illustration contained in Mr. Zauderer's ad. Given those discernible, provable benefits, as well as other less direct benefits that may incidentally have led to the Robbins ad and the ultimate recall, it's important to note that the appellee at the trial offered no evidence whatsoever of any harms that resulted or indeed that could result from the running of this Dalkon shield ad. None of appellants' clients ever came forward with a complaint. No one complained about him or his services, and indeed, all of the harms that appellee even suggests in his brief in this court are hypothetical and admitted by appellee not to apply to the facts of this case. The question then becomes, does the First Amendment permit the state of Ohio to discipline a lawyer for running this truthful ad? And to analyze that question, we must go through the analysis in Central Hudson of determining whether the interest is substantial, whether the interest of the state is directly advanced by these prohibitions and are the prohibitions more restrictive than necessary? Now, turning first to the solicitation charges, we agree with the appellee that advertising is simply one means by which lawyers solicit clients. But that, of course, is only the beginning of the inquiry, for advertising is precisely what was done in Bates and RMJ, advertising in the mass media as it was true here. And in those cases, the court said that the advertisements could not be prohibited consistent with the First Amendment. The only difference between those cases and this is that here the advertisement is directed toward clients who are interested in potentially suing a particular company over a particular medical device. But we believe that that principle has no basis for distinguishing this case from the others. Principally because the state has been unable to identify any legitimate interest that it has in protecting an individual defendant as opposed to the public at large. At trial, it offered no evidence in support of this restriction at all. In its brief in this court, it suggests that the purpose of this restriction is to deter frivolous or malicious lawsuits. We agree, of course, that deterring that kind of litigation is a proper end for the state in various forms of regulation. But there's no reason to believe that the anti-solicitation prohibitions as they are applied to mass media in this case has any likelihood of decreasing that kind of improper activity, particularly because in contingency cases such as this, the lawyer will be paid only if he can prevail. Now, in addition, there are substantial reasons to believe that there are other alternatives far less restrictive than the prohibitions here that would enable the state to protect its interests. I point to three in this particular context. Malicious prosecution and abusive process lawsuits, sanctions under Ohio Rule 11, which is the counterpart of Federal Rule 11 of the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure, and of course, and most important of all, direct discipline against the attorney who persisted in bringing malicious or unwarranted actions. Now, there is another aspect of this matter that undercuts the point that the appellees rely on. As this court recognized in Bates, the major problem for individuals who seek services of a lawyer is that they are unable to find the right lawyer to do their case at a price that they can afford. And here, appellee has bridged that gap by telling prospective clients, I am available, I am doing these kind of cases, and I am willing to do them for you on a contingent fee basis. yet Ohio seems to be saying that it would be proper to advertise for product liability suits in general, but that it is improper to be more specific and to be more helpful. To us, that turns the First Amendment and Bates on its head, and we submit that neither authority nor logic supports that kind of distinction. Mr. Morris, may I interrupt you with a question? What is your position if this had been done in face-to-face meetings orally? He knew that there were 20 women who had purchased this device, and he went to call on each one of them, gave precisely the same message. That, of course, is one step this side of the Oralic case where the court was faced with in-person solicitation by a lawyer of a recent accident victim while in the hospital. my own view is that in-person solicitation is not necessarily something that can be prohibited or that ought to be prohibited. Nonetheless, I recognize that there are substantial potential dangers from in-person solicitation in the form of overreaching, in the form of persuading a person to sign a piece of paper that would retain the lawyer at that particular time. My own view would be that it would be very important for the court to explore other alternatives in determining whether the absolute prohibition applied. But I think that there is a clear line both in terms of evidentiary basis for determining what the lawyer said as opposed to a written matter where there is no problem. With respect to the clear line, which side of the line would the case fall on if instead of a general ad like this, you had a mailing list with about 25 people's names. I believe that a mailing list is constitutionally protected. It's clearly like this case. It is. That indeed, if Mr. Zouder had Xeroxed the ad which he had here and he knew, for instance, or he simply, he knew, for instance, that there were people who had used Dalkon Shield IUDs, although in this case it's not clear how he would do that, but he simply engaged in test mailing. He sent it to occupant such and such an address. It seems to me hard to understand how the fact that it was a, it came in in a Xeroxed envelope, in an envelope, as opposed to coming in the newspaper to the door, would have any bearing on it. Nonetheless, there are some cases which suggest that there may be potential conflicts of interest, that is, when the solicitation came out, for instance, through a real estate broker for a lawyer advertising for real estate services. That might cause some concern, but under the facts and circumstances here, I don't think that that would be a problem. And I think there's a very important lesson from Bates that pushes you in the direction of not insisting that lawyers limit the means by which they make initial contact with the client. And that is, as the court recognized in Bates, the advertisement or the in-person solicitation or the letter is simply the first step in the process by which a lawyer-client relationship is established. And that most people today do not hire lawyers on the basis of ads, on the basis of a letter in the paper, or just because a friend had referred them to. They are much more sophisticated, and they will take the time to find out whether this is the right lawyer. In addition, it seems to me, and this is a point that I want to make in connection with the contingent fee disclosure requirements, that the state's interest ought to focus on the time when the lawyer-client relationship is crystallized in the form of an agreement. And if the state is truly concerned about misrepresentations, not clear about what the terms of the agreement are, the best and surest way to avoid that and the way most consistent with the First Amendment is for the state to require that fee agreements be in writing and that in contingent fee areas they clearly disclose the kind of factors which the state of Ohio insists must go in the initial contact, in the ad. That seems to me far more closely tailored to satisfy the ends of the state and far more consistent with the approach of the First Amendment that information, by and large, is something we should want to get out. We should want in your times running. There was another violation found here, that against misleading advertisements not related to the Dawkins Shield. And the only sanction here was a reprimand, was it not? That is correct. Well, if that reprimand must be sustained under the charge of violation against misleading advertisements, why do we have to get into any of the Dawkins Shield organs? Well, that of course assumes that the ad relating to drunk driving could also be sustained. And as I've indicated in my brief and prepared to discuss, there are very serious due process problems relating to notice and the opportunity to be heard. But even then, I would say, I think a fair reading of the history of this case indicates that the proceeding would never have been brought against Mr. Zowder but for the Dawkins Shield ad. and that the ads relating to the drunk driving matters was a throw in it. Well, suppose we conclude that the misleading advertisement conclusion has to stand. Then what do we do? I would say that in any event... Affirm the judgment? I would say it ought to be, the case ought to be remanded to the Ohio Supreme Court for it to exercise its discretion to determine whether they wish to impose a public reprimand on the appellant given the circumstances of this... Now, isn't that the mildest form of sanction they can impose? But he seems... Or if we send it back, you can't do better than it's been done. They could... I believe they have the authority to dismiss the entire proceeding. But in any event, I would point out, Your Honor, that under Ohio law, even though a public reprimand sounds relatively modest, it is a serious matter to Mr. Zauderer first. And second, and probably more important, is that if he were ever to be subjected again to the slightest infraction, he would automatically lose his license for a year. And that's a very serious matter. So that it seems to me under the circumstances that it would be singly appropriate for the court to remand the matter to the Ohio Supreme Court for it to review it in light of the court's disposition with respect to the Dalton Shields. Well, in effect, the effect of the judgment is to prevent him from publishing ads like this. It's prevent him from doing anything that he may be arguably close to the line, even when he believes that it's in his best interest with the client, because he cannot risk having another proceeding brought against. So you think, realistically, that there's something more involved in this case than the suspension? Oh, yes. In the sense that he will be prevented from... Absolutely. And so will other lawyers in the state of Ohio. in the... I'm sorry. It's only a reprimand. You're... I mean a reprimand. Yes, I was agreeing with Justice White that there was more and I was not focusing on the more than what, and I beg your pardon on that. But there's more involved than just a reprimand. Certainly is. And there's a continuing matter for him as to whether he can take out ads of this kind in similar situations so that he does have that and that is quite correct. With respect to the drunk driving ad, it seems to me it's very important to note that he was charged on one theory. Apelli now agrees that the theory on which he was convicted was another one and that the change involved an entirely different basis for... There was no change in the rule. There was no change in the rule. There was no change in the ad. It's almost an analogy of somebody who was charged with a tax violation, an income tax violation, and the case is brought on a net worth basis and they suddenly find that they're trying it on a cash basis. And he says, wait a second, I was all prepared to put evidence in on this. He never had a chance to say what he would have done in this case if in fact somebody had pled to a lesser... On the drunk driving charge, it appeared to me very funny that you can, without any prohibition, advertise that if you lose the case you give back the fee. Well, the state initially said that that was an offer for contingency in a criminal case. We disputed that and said as a matter of Ohio law that there is a difference. Both the Board of Grievances and the Ohio Supreme Court, in our view, implicitly rejected the equation of the two by going on the other theory, the theory which had not been urged by a pelly, despite the fact that the case had been brought and tried on that basis. And we think at the very least he's entitled to go back and put on, to find out what these municipal reports are, to go back and see what they show, to have them identify, and to be able to take the stand and explain what he would have done in the event that that situation. Mr. Zardo has written a letter of apology to the Board saying that he believes that that language was infelicitous. That wasn't his word, but it's surely the sense of his letter. He had not focused on the matter when he put the ad out. He's expressed his regret. That appeared to be enough until the Dalkon Shield ad came along and he was charged with violations based on that. Thank you, Your Honor. I'll reserve the remainder of my time. Mr. Farr. Thank you, Mr. Chief Justice. May it please the Court. This case is very different from the lawyer advertising cases previously before this Court. It does not involve a ban on advertising itself, as did Bates, or a ban on advertising easily verifiable information, as did RMJ. Ohio allows such advertising and more. What Ohio does not allow, and what this case is about, is for lawyers to entice clients with three particular selling tools. The first is unsolicited legal advice given as part of a direct appeal for business. The second is incomplete information about contingent fees. And the third are pictures and illustrations. And as I shall discuss, each of these choices protects the public from lawyers overreaching and possible misleading appeals in a narrow and reasonable way. Now, I'd like to turn... if we have to sustain the violation based on misleading advertising? The judgment may be sustained on any of the violations found by the Supreme Court. Why should we get into all of this if we have to sustain it on the misleading advertising? If you agree with us on the drunk driving ad or on any one of these points, you need not get into the rest. Mr. Farr, is that quite right? Let me just ask you this question. Public reprimand, has it been given yet? Yes, it has. It's been published in the Ohio Reports, I believe. And does not the reprimand condemn him for more than one misdeed? The reprimand discloses the various basis of the violation. And doesn't it say that he did wrong in more than one respect? The opinion goes into that discussion. And if part of what he did was constitutionally protected and therefore not wrong, would it not be necessary to reduce the scope of the reprimand? Well, I believe that the public reprimand is simply a generic discipline and that the Ohio Supreme Court would not have to, for example, write another opinion if this court remanded in the belief that one of the grounds of discipline was unconstitutional. I think they could give a public reprimand, as that is generically known, for discipline on any one of these violations, regardless of the others. And I think the opinion is just a general explanation. And you think it's a matter of law that a reprimand for committing 97 different offenses is no more serious than a reprimand for just the drunk driving? I think that's correct, Your Honor. Now, I would like to turn first to the restriction on giving legal advice as part of a direct appeal for business. And that is the restriction that is found in Rule 2104 at page 29A of the appendix to the jurisdictional statement. Now, it's important to understand just what Section 104 involves. What it prohibits and what appellant conceitedly did here is for a lawyer to accept employment resulting from the giving of unsolicited legal advice to a layman. It does not bar the giving of advice to a layman who asks for it. And because of exception 4 to the same rule, it does not bar writing or speaking publicly on legal matters so long as the lawyer doesn't tout himself in the bargain. It is only the combination of first, giving the unsolicited legal advice and second, making it part of a direct appeal for business that Ohio prohibits. And even then, it only prohibits the conduct of accepting employment, not the speech itself. Now, we state, excuse me, we submit that the state has a vital interest in barring the use of legal advice as part of a selling pitch. First of all, at the core of any attorney-client relationship is the expectation that the lawyer will give objective, disinterested legal advice. Advertising, by its very nature, is not disinterested. The purpose of advertising is to make the product hear the bringing of litigation by appellant seem as attractive as possible, if not more so. So when a lawyer gives legal advice, not part of his general obligation to inform the public on legal subjects by writing or speaking publicly, but when he gives it as part of a direct appeal for business, it's the goal of that legal advice to excite an interest in litigation or whatever legal services the lawyer is offering. Under those circumstances, there is a serious and unacceptable risk that the lawyer will tailor the legal advice more for his own benefit than for the benefit of the client's. Now, I'd like to point out that this use of legal advice, if allowed, is hard to defend against. We are not talking about a standardized product or one which consumers use frequently on a retail basis. Legal advice is hard to understand, particularly where it involves, as it does here, complex matters of product liability, medical malpractice, and the sort. Few readers will have the kind of expertise that will help them sort out what might be puffing in the legal advice from the core of correct legal advice. Furthermore, this is not the kind of information that consumers can readily test for themselves. Trial and error does not work in the context of legal advice as it does with shampoos or other products. And even if it did, it would be an unattractive and unpleasant way for people to find out that lawyers' advertising claims were false or potentially misleading. Do you feel, Mr. Farr, that the state regulation of this type of thing on the ground that it's misleading then would not accomplish for the state's objective? No, I think that you cannot, you are also aiming at the areas where the risk of approaches to the consumers is high, where the risk that they are misleading or overreaching or overly optimistic is high. I don't think that the information itself has to be found to be misleading. You say the First Amendment allows some prophylactic range for the state? I believe it does. And in fact, I think that's what the court said in Oralik, where it recognized that there may be cases, of course, where even in-person solicitation provides the benefits of advising somebody about their rights. But I think the court made very clear that the state could nonetheless aim at the potential risk by a prophylactic rule. And I think the court did the same thing in Friedman with the Texas Automistry Statute. Trade names may in some cases be informative, but the First Amendment allows some play for the state to regulate in the area of commercial speech. I would also like to point out that this is not the kind of information that can be readily cured by a stream of the same sort of information because of the complexity of legal advice and the subjectivity of legal advice, a barrage of competing legal ads, each one making more representations about the subject which is involved in the ad, is only likely to confuse potential consumers. And that's, of course, the result that's exactly opposite from what we're trying to do, which is to better inform the public about how to choose a lawyer. Now, appellant has argued, of course, that legal advice is necessary in advertisements to keep the public informed of their rights. And my first answer for that is, as I've just stated, that the cure is worse than the disease. But there is a second answer. For the appellant in Orlick made exactly the same argument attacking exactly the same rule, Ohio's Rule 2104, and the court flatly rejected it. What the court pointed out was that Rule 2104 does not stop any lawyer from advising the public about its rights. What it does prohibit, in the words of the court, is it prohibits him from using the information, that is, the unsolicited legal advice, as bait with which to obtain employment for a fee. Now, the evils of using this kind of bait do not start and stop with in-person solicitation. There are, of course, other evils associated with in-person solicitation, such as invasion of privacy, certain forms of coercion. But the purpose of legal advice and advertisements is to get the lawyer to the stage of in-person solicitation. And how he does that is something that the state has a separate and fully substantial interest in regulating. Given his purpose, a lawyer cannot be expected to give advice and advertisements that will drive people away from his office. For example, pointing out the often very substantial costs and hardships involved with litigation.
